title: J. W. Hampton, Jr., & Co. v. United States
lead: An importer challenges the extra two cents per pound imposed by a presidential tariff adjustment, testing both Congress’s instructions and its protective purpose.

actors.name: J. W. Hampton, Jr., & Co.
actors.role: Importer of barium dioxide into New York.

actors.name: President Calvin Coolidge
actors.role: Issued the proclamation increasing the statutory base duty.

actors.name: Tariff Commission
actors.role: Conducted the mandatory investigation and hearing.

proceedings: A majority of the Customs Court sustained the statute and assessment.
The Court of Customs Appeals affirmed.
The Supreme Court affirmed on April 9, 1928, with no separate opinion reported.
limits: The Court upheld this statutory adjustment mechanism, not independent presidential taxing power or every later tariff program. It did not recalculate production costs or substitute its own rate.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Congress directs bounded adjustments for changing production costs
sections.cue: What policy and safeguards did § 315 supply?
paragraphs: Section 315 of the Tariff Act of 1922 directed equalization of domestic production costs with those in the principal competing foreign country. The President could adjust classifications and increase or decrease duties to implement that policy, but total change could not exceed fifty percent of Congress’s rate. A change took effect thirty days after proclamation.

The inquiry included wages, materials, wholesale prices, foreign governmental or private advantages, and other competitive differences. Before a proclamation the Tariff Commission had to investigate with reasonable public notice, an opportunity to present evidence, and a hearing. It investigated and advised; the President decided the rate. Changed or disappearing cost differences required modification or termination.

Other boundaries barred movement between free and dutiable lists or changes in duty form and preserved applicable ad valorem ceilings. The President could adjust within Congress’s framework, not freely choose taxable articles and types of tax.

sections.title: Coolidge increases barium dioxide duty and Hampton protests
sections.cue: Which part of the assessment did the importer challenge?
paragraphs: President Calvin Coolidge’s May 19, 1924 proclamation stated that the Commission had investigated barium dioxide after notice and hearing, identified Germany as the principal competitor, and found the existing rate inadequate to equalize cost differences. It raised four cents per pound to six, the maximum fifty-percent increase.

J. W. Hampton, Jr., & Co. imported barium dioxide into New York and paid the increased assessment. It challenged authority for the additional two cents, not a fresh judicial calculation of costs. Through prescribed customs review, a majority of the Customs Court upheld § 315; the Court of Customs Appeals affirmed. The Attorney General certified the case’s importance during that process, and the Supreme Court granted review.

Hampton argued first that Congress transferred its legislative taxing power to the President and second that tariffs protecting domestic industry exceeded a supposed revenue-only taxing authority. Chief Justice Taft addressed those constitutional questions separately.

sections.title: Taft finds an intelligible policy with limits and a means of applying it
sections.cue: Why did practical executive judgment not become making the law?
paragraphs: Congress had chosen equalization of production and selling costs for comparable goods in the American market. Measurement might be difficult without making the objective unintelligible. Information might be incomplete initially and costs could later shift, so investigation and recurring adjustment supplied a practical way to execute the selected relationship.

Separation of powers prohibited surrendering legislative power or invading another branch’s constitutional field, but did not demand government without interbranch assistance. Permissible assistance depended on the task and coordinated government’s practical needs. Earlier decisions, including Grimaud and Field, distinguished choosing the governing law from discretion under an enacted rule. Conditional legislation could attach consequences to future facts officials would identify.

Rate regulation illustrated the same division: Congress could not prescribe every interstate carriage rate, but could require just, reasonable, nondiscriminatory rates and assign investigation and application to a commission. Tariffs were not categorically exempt from executive assistance.

The intelligible-principle requirement meant an enacted principle directing the official, not merely the existence of investigators. Cost equalization supplied the objective; statutory factors, mandatory procedure, the fifty-percent ceiling, and other restrictions bounded response. Field’s reciprocity mechanism supported treating implementation of specified policy as execution, although Hampton involved continuing numerical adjustments with advisory assistance. Authority remained § 315, not a freestanding presidential power to tax.

sections.title: The protective purpose survives a separate constitutional objection
sections.cue: What did the final affirmance leave in place?
paragraphs: Taft then examined Congress’s own power to pursue protection while collecting revenue. Tariff practice beginning with the 1789 Act expressly encouraged manufactures; early legislators familiar with framing and sustained later enactments contradicted a strict revenue-only limitation. Constitutional authority was distinct from whether protection was wise policy.

A measure raising general-government revenue could pursue additional aims through selection of goods and rates. Protection did not erase this Act’s revenue character. Thus Congress could pursue the policy, and the bounded implementation method did not impermissibly transfer legislative power.

On April 9, 1928, the Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Customs Appeals. Six cents per pound remained effective, with no recovery of the challenged increment and no judicial replacement rate. No separate Supreme Court writing was reported; the Customs Court’s divided decision was a different stage. The holding does not decide later tariffs under other statutes.

sources.pinpoint: Protective-purpose reasoning; Judgment; Separate Opinions; 276 U.S. 411–413
